html:
The uprising of Arab forces against the Ottoman Empire during the First World War, launched in June 1916 by Hussein bin Ali, Sharif of Mecca, with British money, guns and advisers.

Britain had promised Hussein, in letters with its official in Cairo, that the Arabs would get independence after the war. His sons Faisal and Abdullah led the tribes of the Hejaz and beyond, among them chiefs like the Ruwala leader of the Bin Sha'lan. The British officer T. E. Lawrence became their best known adviser. The rebels raided the Hejaz Railway again and again, tying down Ottoman troops at Medina. In July 1917 they took the port of Aqaba, and in October 1918 they entered Damascus alongside British forces.

But in 1916 Britain and France had secretly agreed, in the Sykes-Picot deal, to split the region between them. After the war France took Syria and drove out Faisal, who had been crowned king in Damascus. Britain took Palestine and Mesopotamia, and made Faisal king of Iraq and Abdullah emir of Transjordan, today's Jordan. Hussein's own kingdom of the Hejaz fell to Ibn Saud in 1925.

The revolt became a founding story of Arab nationalism, and also a story of betrayal.
sum: The uprising of Arab forces against the Ottoman Empire during the First World War, launched in June 1916 by Hussein bin Ali, Sharif of Mecca, with British money, guns and advisers.
